# Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 7 (Bi-Vb Pc7)

**ID:** Bi-Vb Pc7
**Section:** Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga (bi-vb)
**Collection:** Vinaya

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** 7. Asking for raw grain
**Title (English, from literature):** Asking for raw grain

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The seventh Pācittiya rule of the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga (*Āmakadhañña*) stipulates that a nun who asks for raw grain (*āmakadhañña*), or has it requested, and then prepares it—by roasting, pounding, or cooking it—and consumes it must confess an offense (*pācittiya*) [SuttaCentral; Hüsken 1997]. According to the origin narrative, during the harvest season (*sassakāle*), nuns who had begged for raw grain were stopped at the city gates by collectors who treated them as peasant women or merchants and demanded toll taxes (*Wegzoll*) [Hüsken 1997]. The regulation was instituted to prevent nuns from being misidentified as traders and to disengage them from resuming the domestic cooking and food preparation tasks typical of household life, closely paralleling the intent of the preceding rule [Hüsken 1997].

In the commentarial tradition, the *Samantapāsādikā* analyzes the rule's terminology (such as *viññāpetvā* in the causative sense of requesting) and explicitly rejects an alternative interpretation found in the older *Mahāpaccarī* commentary regarding whether the act of preparation itself constitutes a *pācittiya* offense [Hüsken 1997].

Curated parallels to this rule are preserved across monastic codes, including the Pali Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha and Parivāra, as well as the Chinese, Tibetan, and Sanskrit recensions of the Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Mahāsāṅghika, and Lokottaravāda traditions [SuttaCentral]. Hüsken observes that while other Vinaya traditions primarily penalize the preparation of raw food rather than the solicitation of raw grain, both traditions address the underlying prohibition [Hüsken 1997]. DharmaNexus records cross-language alignment with the Tibetan *Pratimokṣasūtravṛtti* (D4107) and extensive Pali-internal formulaic reuse across 81 other texts, sharing its largest segments of phrasing with Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiyas 57, 8, 62, 17, and 54 [DharmaNexus].
